Euler Line Simple

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Move the corners of a triangle and watch three special dots line up; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus one and press the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show lines, and press Highlight A, B or C to colour a four-sided shape.

Drag A, B or C, or focus a corner and press the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps).

Look for the math

Three points made from any triangle insist on lying on one straight line. The page's exact claim is that the orthocenter H, the centroid G and the circumcenter O are collinear on the Euler line, and that GH = 2 GO.

How this differs from Euler Collinearity

The other page, Euler Collinearity, starts with any point P, scales the midpoints of the sides from P and asks where three new lines meet; their meeting points form the line GP, which is the Euler line only when P is O. This page proves that the Euler line exists at all. Its proof, due to the Serbian teacher Vladimir Nikolin, uses opposite points on the circle instead of scaled midpoints. The logic test checked the claim here on 5,008 triangles — acute, right, obtuse and very thin — and it held in every one.

A diameter makes a parallelogram

Let F be the point opposite C on the circumcircle, so CF is a diameter. An inscribed angle on a diameter is a right angle, so BF is perpendicular to BC; the altitude AH is perpendicular to BC too, hence AH and BF are parallel. In the same way AF is parallel to BH. So AFBH is a parallelogram: its diagonals AB and FH cross at their shared midpoint, the midpoint Mc of AB. The applet draws the same picture for A (with D) and for B (with E); with Hint on, Highlight A, B or C picks which one you see.

The same median twice

Now CMc is a median of triangle ABC and also of triangle HFC. In triangle ABC the centroid G cuts it in the ratio CG : GMc = 2 : 1. In triangle HFC the point O is the midpoint of CF, so HO is another median and its meeting point with CMc cuts the same segment in the same ratio — it must be the very same G. That puts G on HO, and because G is twice as close to O as to H, GH = 2 GO.

What is drawn, and one slip in the applet

The five switches are the applet's own: altitudes, medians, perpendicular bisectors, hint and names. The three Highlight buttons stand in for pressing a corner; the applet marks the parallelogram only when a corner has been selected or dragged. In its Hint drawing for C, the applet draws the segment A–Ma where the proof needs the median C–Mc (it kept the line from the A case). We follow the page and draw C–Mc. For three corners in a straight line, or when the applet's line-intersection test returns no point, the circle and Euler line are hidden rather than drawn with impossible coordinates. The logic test also confirmed that D, E and F are the exact antipodes 2O − A, 2O − B, 2O − C, and that each parallelogram's diagonals share a midpoint.

Try dragging C past the opposite side to make an obtuse triangle, then switch between Highlight A, B and C: the shaded four-sided shape changes, but the straight line through H, G and O does not.
